summary: James Russo, co-creator and tech lead of HyperFrames at HeyGen, presents the case that HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are the ideal format for LLM-generated video because they constitute the bulk of LLM training data. The talk chronicles a year-long journey through multiple approaches. After Effects and Premiere Pro produce excellent results but aren't agent-friendly. Lottie and Rive use custom formats that aren't the model's native tongue. Remotion worked but required teaching the framework, which boxed in the agent's creativity. HTML, by contrast, let models naturally produce great output when given examples, especially after Gemini 3's step-function improvement. The key design decision was using Gemini 3 Flash—a small model—as their design partner. If a small model could author workable code, larger models certainly could. To their surprise, the thinnest wrapper won: plain HTML with a few data attributes as metadata for timing. This became HyperFrames, an open-source framework turning agent-authored HTML into video. The hard engineering challenge was deterministic MP4 rendering. Browsers are asynchronous by design—fonts, images, and assets load on their own schedules. For video, every frame must be fully loaded. HyperFrames solves this by freezing the browser's clock and seeking deterministically to each frame, waiting for everything to load, taking a screenshot, and moving on. Anything renderable in a browser—Three.js, WebGL, SVGs, shaders, Lottie—becomes available in video. Rather than teaching agents a framework's syntax, HyperFrames' skills focus on taste and video aspects like motion, composition, and narrative. A single-shot website-to-video skill produces decent results, but great output requires a human-in-the-loop workflow: storyboarding frame-by-frame, adding motion iteratively, and last-mile editing in the HyperFrames studio. Keyframes, released the day of the talk, provide professional motion-design control. Scale metrics include 1.3 million videos rendered in 90 days, 267,000 creators, 15,000 daily renders, and 32,000 GitHub stars. Russo honestly acknowledges that models still aren't good at creative work, and the team is developing a code-to-video benchmark with LLM labs and video agent creators to raise the floor for everyone. The talk closes with the AI Engineer Warfare showcase video created using HyperFrames, and a call to the community to use the open-source framework, download skills, and collaborate.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and HeyGen Mission
sections.summary: Russo opens with an agent-generated video, introduces himself as co-creator of HyperFrames at HeyGen, and frames the problem: coding agents have made building easy, but launching products with great video remains hard. HeyGen's mission is to solve communication through video, starting with AI avatars (A-roll) but requiring B-roll, animations, captions, and music to create complete videos.

sections.title: Why HTML Is the Native Language of LLMs
sections.summary: Russo argues HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are the native languages of LLMs since most training data is web content. Teaching models a custom DSL is like asking Shakespeare to write in Japanese. He notes Karpathy and others independently arrived at similar conclusions about HTML as a new markdown for LLM visual output.

sections.title: Framework Comparison and the Path to HTML
sections.summary: Russo maps frameworks on quality vs agent-friendliness axes. After Effects and Premiere Pro are gold standards but not agent-friendly. Lottie and Rive use custom formats lacking editability. Remotion was promising but required teaching the framework, limiting creativity. After Gemini 3's improvement, models naturally gravitated to HTML when given examples, leading the team to stop fighting the model.

sections.title: Gemini Flash as Design Partner and Thin Wrapper
sections.summary: The team used Gemini 3 Flash as their design partner—if a small model could author workable code, larger models would too. Despite trying many wrappers with large system prompts and skills, the thinnest wrapper won: plain HTML with a few data attributes as metadata. This validated the format and became HyperFrames, an open-source framework.

sections.title: Deterministic Rendering: Freezing the Browser Clock
sections.summary: The hard engineering challenge was turning HTML into deterministic MP4. Browsers load fonts, images, and assets asynchronously—fine for performance, terrible for reproducible pixels. HyperFrames solves this by freezing the browser clock, seeking deterministically to each frame, waiting for all assets to load, taking a screenshot, and repeating. Any browser-renderable technology (Three.js, WebGL, SVGs, shaders, Lottie) becomes available in video.

sections.title: Skills for Taste, Not Syntax
sections.summary: HyperFrames skills focus on taste and video aspects because LLMs already know HTML. This differs from other frameworks where skills teach framework syntax. A website-to-video skill demonstrates single-shot capability: given a URL, it retrieves assets and branding, applies motion examples, and produces decent output. Constant evaling with agents raises the floor of base output.

sections.title: Human-in-the-Loop Workflow, Keyframes, and Scale Metrics
sections.summary: Great output requires craft: narrative vision, frame-by-frame storyboarding, iterative motion design, and last-mile editing in the HyperFrames studio. Keyframes were released the day of the talk for professional motion coordination. Scale metrics: 1.3M videos rendered in 90 days, 267K creators, 15K daily renders, 32K GitHub stars. The framework is open-source, free forever, and works with any coding agent.

sections.title: Code-to-Video Benchmark and Closing
sections.summary: Russo honestly admits models still aren't good at creative work despite extensive evaling. To address this at a higher level, the team is developing a code-to-video benchmark with LLM labs and video agent creators to raise the floor for everyone. The AI Engineer Warfare showcase video is presented as a collaboration using HyperFrames. Russo closes with the thesis that agents make building easy but launching hard, and HTML is all agents need to make great videos. He invites the community to use the open-source repo, download skills, and connect.
